It is identified with “Itahato Shrine” of Kasube District, {{ill|Owari Province|Q514506|qid=Q514506}}, in the '{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|Q11064932|qid=Q11064932}}'. {{nihongo|'''Itahato Shrine'''|伊多波刀神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Owari Province]].

== Enshrined deities ==
The principal deities are {{ill|Takamimusubi|qid=Q125400|lt=Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Emperor Ōjin|qid=Q317997|lt=Hondawake-no-Mikoto|qid=Q317997}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Okinagatarashihime-no-Mikoto}}, and the {{ill|Tamayori-hime (mother of Jimmu)|Q3082751|qid=Q3082751|lt=Tamayorihime-no-Mikoto}} “{{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Hachiman Three Deities}}.” Also merged are {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Ōyamazumi-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|Ichikishima-hime|qid=Q11059454|lt=Ichikishimahime-no-Mikoto}}, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Izunome-no-Mikoto}}, and Hondawake-no-Mikoto (same as Hondawake-no-Mikoto).

== History ==
Shrine tradition says it was founded in year 42 of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723}}, but exact founding year is unknown. Until the {{ill|Early modern period|Q5308718|qid=Q5308718}} it was called '''Hachimangū'''. The oldest {{ill|Munafuda|Q8008834|qid=Q8008834}} from {{ill|1523|Q6302|qid=Q6302}} ({{ill|Daiei (era)|Q1193564|qid=Q1193564}} 3) reads “Hachimangū main shrine.” In the early-Edo '{{ill|Kanbunmuramuraoboegaki|Q137766629|qid=Q137766629}},' it appears as “Dairaku Village ... Hachiman ... held by village negi Sukedayū.” In the {{ill|Edo period|lt=Edo period|qid=Q184963}}, it was the {{ill|Ujigami|Q767655|qid=Q767655}} of Dairaku Village in {{ill|Kasugai district|Q11513576|qid=Q11513576}}, and revered as the general {{ill|Ubusunagami|Q1392097|qid=Q1392097}} of 17 villages of Ajioka-shō. Traditions include donation of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shuinchi}} and three sets of {{ill|Japanese armour|Q3671179|qid=Q3671179}} by {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800}} for military fortune; from the {{ill|Middle Ages|Q12554|qid=Q12554}} onward it prospered as a {{ill|Hachiman|ar|هاتشيمان|az|Haçiman|ca|Hachiman|de|Hachiman|el|Χατσίμαν|es|Hachiman|eu|Hachiman|fa|هاچیمان|fi|Hachiman|fr|Hachiman|hu|Hacsiman|id|Hachiman|it|Hachiman|ja|八幡神|ko|하치만 신|mni|ꯍꯆꯤꯃꯥꯟ|my|ဟချိမန်း|pl|Hachiman|pt|Hachiman|ru|Хатиман|simple|Hachiman|sl|Hačiman|sv|Hachiman|tok|jan sewi Kasiman|tr|Hachiman|uk|Хачіман|uz|Hachiman|vi|Hachiman|wuu|八幡神|zh|八幡神|qid=Q261637}} shrine attracting {{ill|Buke|Q2927809|qid=Q2927809}}, and with donations by {{ill|Oda Nobunaga|Q171411|qid=Q171411}} had 5 chō 8 tan of shrine land in the {{ill|Keichō|ca|Keichō|es|Keichō|fa|کیچو (دوره)|fr|Ère Keichō|id|Keichō|it|Keichō|ja|慶長|ko|게이초|ru|Кэйтё|simple|Keichō|sr|Кеичо|sv|Keichō|th|เคโช|tr|Keichō|uk|Кейтьо|zh|慶長|qid=Q1328185}} era, but this was all confiscated by {{ill|kenchi|Q1092846|qid=Q1092846}}. Until early modern times there was {{ill|Jōnen-ji|Q0|qid=Q0|lt=Jōnen-ji}} (now defunct) as its {{ill|Jingū-ji|Q1074971|qid=Q1074971}}.

In mid-Edo, {{ill|Amano Sadakage|Q6535030|qid=Q6535030}} identified it with the Kasube District “Itahato Shrine” in the 'Engishiki Jinmyōchō,' and this became accepted theory. In the '{{ill|Owari Kokunai Jinmyōchō|Q11041830|qid=Q11041830}},' it appears as “Junior Third Rank Itabato Tenjin.” The basis for Amano’s identification is unclear, but he considered a folk custom of drawing {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=pigeons}} on {{ill|board|Q114207382|qid=Q114207382}} and offering them to the deity as the origin of the name{{Sfn|津田正生|1978|p=84}}. {{ill|Tsuda Masanari|Q22123474|qid=Q22123474}} and others questioned this{{Sfn|津田正生|1978|p=84}}, and it has been pointed out that it may derive from association with the pigeon as {{ill|Shinshi|Q10444973|qid=Q10444973}} of Hachiman<ref name="調査報告">'Shikinaisha Survey Report.'</ref>. Takeshi Shiga proposed a theory that it is a transformation of “Itahata,” meaning water-springing fields{{Sfn|加藤宏|1988|p=224}}. According to 'Aichi-ken Gun Chōson Aza-mei Chō' (1882), Dairaku Village had a {{ill|koaza|Q5327509|qid=Q5327509}} called “Hatobe.”

In {{ill|1870|Q7741|qid=Q7741}} (Meiji 3) it was ranked {{ill|Gō-sha|Q134917316|qid=Q134917316}}, and just before abolition of the modern shrine rank system, on Jan. 10, {{ill|1946|Q18610|qid=Q18610}} (Shōwa 21), it was promoted to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Prefectural Shrine}}.

== Rites ==
The {{ill|Reisai|Q11385469|qid=Q11385469}} was originally on old-calendar Aug. 15, later changed to Oct. 5, and now held on the second Monday of October. Until early modern times, {{ill|Yabusame|Q1886157|qid=Q1886157}} was dedicated at the annual festival; it is depicted in '{{ill|Owari meisho zue|Q11465290|qid=Q11465290}}' and said to have been the foremost ceremony in {{ill|Kasugai district|Q11513576|qid=Q11513576}}<ref name="市役所">Kasugai City Hall, “[http://www.city.kasugai.lg.jp/22498/kanko/464/itadojinja.html Itahato Shrine]”.</ref>. Performers wore armor at Jōnen-ji and, after riding three {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=horses}} to worship, dedicated yabusame<ref>'Higashi Kasugai Gun-shi,' Higashi Kasugai District Office, Taishō 12.</ref>. After Meiji it declined and ceased; now only an armored warrior procession, horse-tower by men in unlucky ages, and warrior target-shooting by men in pre-unlucky year remain<ref name="市役所"/>, but this rite was designated a city {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} on Apr. 14, {{ill|1950|Q18597|qid=Q18597}} as “Yabusame Dedicated to Itahato Shrine”<ref>{{Cite web|ja|date=2011-04-01 |url=http://www.city.kasugai.lg.jp/bunka/bunkazai/shinai/shishitei.html |title=List of city-designated cultural properties |publisher=Kasugai City |accessdate=2013-05-27}}</ref>. On that day, local children also gather carrying {{ill|Lion dance|Q713866|qid=Q713866}} and {{ill|Mikoshi|Q979940|qid=Q979940}}.

== Precinct shrines ==
In the precincts are 14 shrines: {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Tsushima Shrine}}, Amaterasu Ōkami Shrine, Toyouke Shrine, Kumano Shrine, Akiba Shrine, Hakusan Shrine, Atsuta Shrine, Atago Shrine, Tado Shrine, Sannō Shrine, Ōhirume Shrine, Sugawara Shrine, Goryō Shrine, Asama Shrine, and Takebe Shrine. Of these, Amaterasu Ōkami Shrine and Toyouke Shrine at the {{ill|Sandō|Q667783|qid=Q667783}} entrance were formerly outside-precinct shrines<ref name="調査報告"/>.

== Precincts ==
The cherry trees along the approach are a noted cherry-viewing spot in the city<ref>Aichi Prefecture Parks and Greenery Division, “[http://www.pref.aichi.jp/koen/keikanshigen/kasugai/021.html Cherry trees of Itahato Shrine, Kasugai City]”.</ref>.

On the right side facing the main sanctuary is a lantern donated by Sasada Denzāemon and others<ref>{{Cite web |title=Tomichū Akitomo, “Following Sasada Denzāemon of Dairaku no Suya,” 'Kasugai Kyōdo-shi' No.7, Kasugai Local History Society |url=https://www.md.ccnw.ne.jp/hondacb/SUYA.htm |website= |access-date=2025-05-18}}</ref>. Sasada Denzāemon became adopted into the Sasada family in Dairaku village (his mother’s birthplace) and brewed vinegar. Later he moved to Fukuro-machi, Nagoya, and opened Suya. Further, the 3rd Sasada Denzāemon absorbed the Okada family (main Suya line) and took the name Suya Kanzaburō. In Meiji, the trademark “Marukan” was approved and registered as supplier to the Imperial Household Ministry. This became today’s Marukan Vinegar company. The main Sasada family line still remains in Kamidairaku-chō.

== Access ==
* {{ill|Meitetsu Bus|Q6810397|qid=Q6810397}}: from {{ill|Kachigawa Station|Q5359249|qid=Q5359249}} to {{ill|Komaki Station|Q6428074|qid=Q6428074}}, get off at “Machiya.”

* Meitetsu Bus: from {{ill|Kasugai Station (JR Central)|Q5359327|qid=Q5359327|lt=Kasugai Station}} to Ōkusa, get off at “Machiya.”
* Meitetsu Bus: from Kasugai Station to Komaki Station, get off at “Nishi-Machiya.”
* {{ill|Komaki Jyunkai Bus|Q11266831|qid=Q11266831}}: Tōkadai line from Komaki Station to Tōkadai Center-kami, get off at “Kamidairaku.”
